title: English Vocabulary in Use — Elementary · Units 41–42 (editorially reviewed)
description: Unit 41 teaches common uses of make/made/made for preparing, producing, feelings and fixed expressions, including contrasts with do and take. Unit 42 covers come/came/come for direction, entry, exit, returning, origins and invitations. English examples and usage notes accompany Brazilian Portuguese translations in pt.
sourceNotice: The instructional and exercise pages, illustrations and common-mistakes boxes from the supplied textbook were inspected. Definitions, notes and example sentences are editorially written; the textbook exercises and illustrations are not reproduced. Where appropriate, exercise-origin items and independently explained dictionary extensions are identified by contentOrigin.

units.title: Unit 41 — Make / made / made
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use Elementary, 3rd ed., Unit 41, textbook pp. 88–89 (PDF pp. 89–90); original example sentences and English-language explanatory notes.
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Elementary (3rd edition)

items.example: They made a short film last summer.
items.note: Make is irregular: make (base form), made (past simple), made (past participle). Use make to prepare food or drinks and to create or produce something.

items.example: I will make some coffee before the meeting.
items.note: Make coffee means prepare it; have coffee generally means drink it. Coffee is usually uncountable when referring to the drink in general.

items.example: Could you make some tea for our guests?
items.note: Use make to prepare a drink: make some tea. Compare have some tea when you mean drink it.

items.example: She makes hot chocolate on cold evenings.
items.note: Make hot chocolate describes preparing the drink. Have hot chocolate usually describes drinking it.

items.example: My father makes breakfast on Sundays.
items.note: Make breakfast means prepare the meal; have breakfast means eat it. Breakfast is usually used without an article in these phrases.

items.example: I made lunch for the children today.
items.note: Make lunch describes preparing the meal. Have lunch means eat lunch.

items.example: He is making dinner for his friends tonight.
items.note: Make dinner describes preparing the meal. Have dinner means eat dinner; making dinner describes an action in progress.

items.example: I made a cup of tea for my grandmother.
items.note: Use make a cup of tea when preparing one cup. This phrase is reinforced in exercise 41.1.

items.pt: fazer uma fotocópia; tirar uma cópia
items.example: Please make a photocopy of this letter.
items.note: Say make a photocopy of a document, but take a photo of a person or place. The two nouns take different verbs.

items.example: The students are making a film about their school.
items.note: Make a film means produce or create one; watch a film means view it.

items.pt: fazer; gravar ou produzir um vídeo
items.example: We are making a video for the school project.
items.note: Use make a video when producing or recording a video. The source presents make a film / video together.

items.example: My brother is making dinner at the moment.
items.note: Drop the final silent e before -ing: make → making. Use am/is/are making for actions happening now.

items.pt: fazer alguém se sentir de determinada maneira
items.example: Long meetings sometimes make people feel tired.
items.note: Pattern: make + person + (feel) + adjective. Both make someone tired and make someone feel tired are possible. Do not add to before feel.

items.example: Working all day without a break makes me tired.
items.note: You can omit feel: a long journey makes me tired. Use makes, not make, after a singular third-person subject.

items.example: The unfair decision made me feel angry.
items.note: Make someone angry and make someone feel angry both describe what causes the feeling. Made expresses the past.

items.example: That story made me sad.
items.note: Make me sad describes a cause of sadness; be sad describes the feeling itself. Feel can be omitted.

items.example: Seeing my friends again made me happy.
items.note: The adjective happy follows me or feel: make me happy; make me feel happy. This adjective is practised in exercise 41.2.

items.pt: me fazer passar mal; me causar enjoo
items.example: That horrible smell made me feel sick.
items.note: In British English, feel sick can mean feel nauseous. The feeling is caused by something; this pattern is practised in exercise 41.2.

items.pt: fez com que eu me sentisse...
items.example: The good news made me feel excited.
items.note: Made is the past tense of make. Use made + person + (feel) + adjective: the news made me happy. Feel is optional in this pattern.

items.example: I made a mistake in the first question.
items.note: Say make a mistake, not do a mistake. The plural is make mistakes; the past is made a mistake or made mistakes.

items.pt: marcar uma consulta; agendar um horário
items.example: I need to make an appointment with the dentist.
items.note: Make an appointment with a doctor or another professional to arrange a meeting at a particular time.

items.example: I make my bed before leaving the house.
items.note: Make your bed means arrange the sheets and covers after sleeping; it does not mean manufacture a bed.

items.example: The children were making a noise in the classroom.
items.note: Say make a noise or make a lot of noise, not do a noise. Noise can be countable or uncountable depending on its meaning.

items.example: The children made a mess in the kitchen.
items.note: Make a mess means create untidiness. A mess is different from a noise, though both commonly follow make.

items.example: You made a good choice when you bought that coat.
items.note: Make a good choice means choose well. Good modifies choice; the verb remains make.

items.example: We need to make a choice before Friday.
items.note: Make a choice means choose between alternatives. In exercise 41.1, learners practise the form make our choice.

items.example: Our neighbours made a lot of noise last night.
items.note: A lot of noise refers to a large amount of sound. This longer expression appears in exercise 41.1.

items.section: Common mistakes · Make, do and take
items.example: Did you do your homework before dinner?
items.note: Use do your homework, not make your homework. Homework is normally uncountable: some homework, not a homework.

items.section: Common mistakes · Make, do and take
items.example: I am going to take an exam next week.
items.note: Take an exam means sit an examination as a candidate. The source also accepts do an exam, but not make an exam in this meaning.

items.pt: fazer uma prova; realizar um exame
items.section: Common mistakes · Make, do and take
items.example: The class did an exam on Monday.
items.note: Do an exam is possible for a student completing an examination; take an exam is also standard. Do not use make an exam for this meaning.

items.section: Common mistakes · Make, do and take
items.example: Could you take a photo of our family?
items.note: Say take a photo, not make a photo. Compare make a film or make a video when producing moving images.

items.section: Common mistakes · Make, do and take
items.example: I do the washing every Saturday.
items.note: In British English, do the washing usually means wash clothes. Do the washing-up typically means wash dishes.

learningObjectives: Use the irregular forms make, made and made, together with the -ing form making.
Use make in common food, drink and production collocations: make coffee or tea, make breakfast, make a photocopy and make a film or video.
Express the cause of a feeling with make + person + (feel) + adjective, including tired, angry, sad, happy and sick.
Use make a mistake, make an appointment, make your bed, make a noise, make a mess and make a choice correctly.
Distinguish make from do and take in common-mistakes examples: do homework, take or do an exam, take a photo and do the washing.
Choose suitable present, past and continuous forms of make in contexts based on exercises 41.1–41.4.

units.title: Unit 42 — Come / came / come
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use Elementary, 3rd ed., Unit 42, textbook pp. 90–91 (PDF pp. 91–92); original example sentences and English-language explanatory notes.
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Elementary (3rd edition)

items.example: My cousin came to our house yesterday.
items.note: Come is irregular: come (base form), came (past simple), come (past participle). Unlike go, come usually describes movement towards the speaker or another relevant place.

items.pt: vir (em direção ao ponto de referência) versus ir (afastando-se dele)
items.example: Please come here; I need to show you something.
items.note: Come usually means move towards the speaker or a reference point; go usually means move away from that point. The choice depends on the situation.

items.example: I heard a knock and said, “Come in!”
items.note: Come in is a common invitation to enter a room, for example after someone knocks on the door. It can be used without an object.

items.example: The teacher came into the classroom at nine.
items.note: Use into before a named place: come into the room. Into describes movement from outside to inside.

items.example: Please wait until everyone comes out.
items.note: Come out describes movement from inside to outside and can be used without saying the place.

items.pt: sair de um lugar; sair de dentro de algo
items.example: A woman came out of the shop carrying two bags.
items.note: Use out of to name the place someone or something leaves: come out of a shop or come out of a machine.

items.word: the ticket comes out of the machine
items.ipa: /ðə ˈtɪkɪt kʌmz aʊt əv ðə məˈʃiːn/
items.example: The ticket comes out of the machine after you pay.
items.note: This example illustrates come out of for movement from inside a machine. The third-person singular form is comes.

items.example: Come here and look at this drawing.
items.note: Here is an adverb of place, so say come here, not come to here. The imperative is practised in exercise 42.2.

items.example: She went away on Friday and came back on Sunday.
items.note: Come back means return to the speaker’s location or another reference point. The past form is came back.

items.example: We came back from Greece last night.
items.note: Use from to identify the place someone returns from: come back from Italy or come back from holiday.

items.pt: voltar para casa (em direção à casa de referência)
items.example: I usually come home at six o’clock.
items.note: Home acts as a direction word in this phrase: say come home, not come to home. The reference point is someone’s home.

items.example: We came home late after the concert.
items.note: Come home late describes returning home at a late time. Late here is an adverb; lately has a different meaning.

items.example: Are you coming back next weekend?
items.note: Are you coming back? is a natural question about a planned return. This future use of the present continuous is reinforced in exercise 42.1.

items.example: My new colleague comes from Italy.
items.note: Use come from to describe someone’s place of origin: I come from Poland. The source warns against using I am coming from for this stable meaning.

items.pt: De onde você é?; de onde você vem?
items.example: Where do you come from? I come from Brazil.
items.note: This question normally asks about a person’s country or place of origin. From comes at the end of the question.

items.example: We are going to the cinema; would you like to come along?
items.note: Come along means accompany someone or join an activity, as in the invitation Do you want to come along?

items.pt: vir visitar alguém; vir ver alguém
items.example: Come and see us when you visit London.
items.note: Come and see someone can mean visit that person. And links two base verbs and is often pronounced with a weak vowel.

items.pt: vir a uma festa; comparecer a uma festa
items.example: Are you coming to the party on Friday?
items.note: Use come to + an event to describe attending it. To is needed here, unlike in come home or come here. The phrase is practised in exercise 42.3.

items.pt: vir buscar algo; vir por algum motivo
items.example: I came for my keys because I left them here.
items.note: Come for can express the purpose of a visit, such as collecting an item. Exercise 42.3 uses this construction.

items.example: Did you come to the meeting yesterday?
items.note: In past-simple questions, use did + base form come, never did + came. This form is reinforced in exercise 42.3.
items.speechText: Did you come to the party?

items.pt: passar na casa de alguém; vir visitar (uso informal britânico)
items.section: Over to you · Dictionary extension (not defined by textbook)
items.example: Would you like to come round for coffee tomorrow?
items.note: PEDAGOGICAL EXTENSION: In informal British English, come round can mean visit someone’s home. The book names this expression as a dictionary task without defining it.

items.section: Over to you · Dictionary extension (not defined by textbook)
items.example: I came across an interesting article while studying.
items.note: PEDAGOGICAL EXTENSION: Come across something can mean find or encounter it by chance. The book asks learners to look the expression up rather than teaching this definition.

items.section: Over to you · Dictionary extension (not defined by textbook)
items.example: An unexpected problem came up during the meeting.
items.note: PEDAGOGICAL EXTENSION: Come up can mean arise or occur, especially of a topic, issue or event. The book mentions the expression for dictionary research but does not define it.

learningObjectives: Recognise the irregular forms come, came and come and distinguish come from go using the speaker’s reference point.
Use come in, come into, come out and come out of when describing movement between inside and outside.
Describe returning with come back, come back from and come home, without adding to before home or here.
Ask and answer questions about origin with come from and Where do you come from?, using the present simple for a stable origin.
Use come along and come and see someone in invitations and come to or come for in suitable contexts.
Recognise come round, come across and come up as dictionary-research suggestions; distinguish supplied explanatory meanings from textbook teaching.
Apply present, past and present-continuous forms of come in contexts based on exercises 42.1–42.4.
